style: Natural, high-quality look. Never dark, moody or cinematic unless Dag asks.
Keep greens true to life. Vivid is fine, neon or fake-looking is not.
Keep Dag's composition. Light crops only, and keep the subject on the third he framed it on.
Leave real details alone (carabiners, gear). Only remove what Dag asks to remove.
Retouching stays light: soften wrinkles and veins, keep skin texture, never touch eyebrows, eyes or lips.
Brighten harsh shadows a little and keep highlights from blowing out.
Background blur stays subtle and natural, never a cutout or portrait-mode look.
gear: Canon camera (stock lens, no ND filter assumed) and iPhone. Lightroom on phone. No lights or gimbal.

profile.summary: You shoot travel and the outdoors, usually a person seen from behind facing a big view, often backlit at sunrise or golden hour. Your best numbers come from named places posted as carousels with a title card.
signature: People from behind looking at the view (Golden Hours, #blue, Rainier, the trail and forest photos)
Backlit sunrise and golden-hour light with the sun in frame
Named places: Tetons, Vancouver, LA, Miami
Warm highlights, either natural or a faded film look

findings.text: Carousels averaged about 3,900 views. Single videos averaged about 2,100. That's roughly 1.8x.
findings.basis: Your 9 posts. Small sample, different places and dates, so treat it as a lean, not a rule.

findings.text: Place-name title cards (Tetons, LA) are in your top 4 by views.
Golden-hour and backlit posts get the most sends per view (Golden Hours 0.26%, Miami 0.20%). Sends are one of Instagram's top three ranking signals.
findings.basis: Your posts + Mosseri via Social Media Today

findings.text: Your lowest post (Glacier) is also your flattest: lowest color (0.10) and lowest contrast of all 8 measured.
Tetons got 2.3% likes per view, your best. Big, clear, layered landscape plus a title.

limits: No ND filter: in bright daylight video, use the 180° rule anyway (1/50 at 24fps) and close the aperture, or shoot near golden hour when light is lower.
Sun in frame blows out on your Canon: expose for the sky (-1 to -2 EV) and lift the shadows in edit.
Phone edits: every recipe below is done in Lightroom mobile or in the app's Apply button.

rubric.name: Light
rubric.what: Direction and quality. Backlit, side, or golden-hour light scores high. Flat midday or overcast scores low.

rubric.name: Exposure
rubric.what: No blown sun or sky, no crushed blacks where detail matters.

rubric.name: Color
rubric.what: One clear, cohesive palette. Subtle grading: a little goes a long way.

rubric.name: Composition
rubric.what: Clear subject, leading lines, layers front to back, a level horizon.

rubric.name: Story
rubric.what: You can tell where this is and why it matters: a named place, a person, a moment.

rubric.name: Instagram fit
rubric.what: 4:5 feed size, carousel or Reel, built to earn likes and sends per view.

recipes.name: Natural (house look)
recipes.when: Most hikes and trips. What you picked on Oct 21.
recipes.doing_well: Tetons and Seaplanes, your top 2, are both natural color.
shoot: Shoot the light, not just the view: morning or late afternoon beats noon.
Keep the person on a third and let the trail or road lead to them.
Expose so the sky isn't white; you can lift shadows later.
edit: Vibrance +10, Saturation 0. Pull Green saturation -5 if it looks neon.
recipes.why: Adobe's color grading guide: small moves have a strong effect.

recipes.name: Golden hour backlight
recipes.when: Sunrise, sunset, someone facing the sun. Your signature.
recipes.doing_well: Golf, #blue, Golden Hours and Rainier all use it. Golden Hours has your best sends per view.
shoot: Put the sun just off the person's head or at the frame edge.
Dial exposure compensation -1 to -2 so the sky keeps color.
White balance Daylight or Shade (not Auto) to keep the warmth.
Hide part of the sun behind a tree or the person to control flare.
edit: Color Grading: Highlights toward orange, saturation 10-15.
Brush the sun area -0.3 exposure so it isn't a white hole.
recipes.why: Nikon's backlighting guide: -1 to -2 EV, Daylight/Shade WB, nudge temperature warmer in post.

recipes.name: Cinematic
recipes.when: Reels and short films where you want a movie feel.
recipes.doing_well: Golf's warm-highlight, cool-shadow grade is your closest so far.
shoot: Film 24fps at 1/50 shutter (the 180° rule) for natural motion blur.
Without an ND filter, shoot near golden hour so you can keep 1/50.
Slow, steady moves: walk slow, pan slow, hold each shot 3-5 seconds.
edit: HSL: Blue hue left, Aqua hue right (teal).
Color Grading: Highlights toward orange, Shadows toward teal. Keep saturation low (5-15).
For video, add 2.39 bars only on widescreen cuts, never on Reels.
recipes.why: Tuts+ orange-and-teal steps, the 180° rule for motion, and Adobe's warning to keep grades subtle.

source.name: Envato Tuts+: Orange and teal look in Lightroom

also.name: Australian Photography: The 180 degree shutter rule

recipes.name: Travel carousel
recipes.when: Any named place. Your best format.
recipes.doing_well: Tetons (5.3K) and LA (3K) both open with a place-name title card.
shoot: Get 5 shots per place: a wide establishing shot, a detail, a person in the scene, a golden-hour shot, and a closer.
Leave empty sky or wall in the first shot for the title.
Shoot vertical or leave room to crop 4:5.
edit: Slide 1: title card with the place name in one clean font.
Same recipe on every slide so the set matches.
recipes.why: 4:5 fills the most screen and survives the new 3:4 grid. Likes and sends per view drive reach.

recipes.name: Faded film
recipes.doing_well: Somewhere in LA (3K views) uses it.
shoot: Look for bold color against plain sky or walls.
edit: Lift blacks (Tone Curve: raise the bottom point a little).
Highlights toward warm in Color Grading.
recipes.why: Lifted blacks and warm highlights are the classic film-stock look. Keep it subtle per Adobe.

recipes.name: Blue hour
recipes.when: Before sunrise or after sunset, mountains and clouds.
shoot: Expose for the sky and let the person go to silhouette.
Brace the camera on a rock; light is low.
edit: Temp -5 to -10, Tint +5 toward magenta for the purple.
Shadows toward blue, Highlights toward pink/orange in Color Grading.
recipes.why: Same backlight exposure rule as golden hour, cooler balance.

research.title: What Instagram ranks on
research.takeaway: Instagram's head says the top 3 ranking signals are watch time, likes and sends. Check likes per reach and sends per reach in your Insights.

research.title: Feed size after the 3:4 grid
research.takeaway: Post at 1080x1350 (4:5). It fills the most screen and still looks right in the new 3:4 profile grid.

research.title: Backlit golden hour
research.takeaway: Sun just off to the side or behind the subject, -1 to -2 EV, Daylight or Shade white balance, then warm it a touch in edit.

research.title: Orange and teal, step by step
research.takeaway: Shift blues toward teal in HSL, push highlights toward orange and shadows toward teal in Color Grading, then save it as a preset.
research.source: Envato Tuts+: Orange and teal look in Lightroom

research.title: Snow reads gray
research.takeaway: Cameras make snow gray, so add +1/3 to +2 EV, and warm the white balance to remove the blue cast on sunny days.

practice.technique: Snow: remove blue cast, keep texture
practice.note: First try followed the +EV tip and blew the snow out to pure white, so the tracks disappeared. Second try only neutralized the blue cast, pulled the brightest snow down and added a little local contrast. Tracks read better. It's a small gain because the screenshot is low quality.

First edit, done live with Dag. Moody grade, carabiner removal and a darker sky were all rejected. What he approved: natural color, greens pulled back, brighter shadows, a light crop keeping Isaiah on the right third, and a gentle background blur that keeps both hikers sharp.

practice.technique: 4:5 crop, tame sun patches, warm touch
practice.note: Cropped vertical with him centered so the trunks frame him. Pulled down the bright sun patches on the bark, brightened the opening behind him, toned down the white towel and added a little warmth. The first try looked hazy, so contrast was added back.
Opened up the shadows a little and kept the sun flare. Background blur was tried and dropped: on a backlit valley it made the whole shot look hazy and washed out.
Softened forehead lines and the wrinkles around his eyes and cheeks with frequency separation, keeping skin texture. Eyes, brows, beard and expression untouched.

Removed the forehead vein and softened wrinkles. First pass smoothed her eyebrows away, which Dag caught; brows are now protected and the smoothing is lighter. Cropped 4:5 to show less fence and tree.

playbook.title: Subject-aware background blur
playbook.how: Mask the people, then blur the background a little more the farther it is from them. Keeps texture near the subject so it looks like real lens falloff.

playbook.title: Light skin retouch
playbook.how: Remove only mid-size detail (wrinkles, veins) and keep fine pore texture. Protect brows, eyes and lips.

playbook.title: Shadow lift without haze
playbook.how: Lift only the deepest shadows and add back gentle contrast. A big lift on a backlit shot looks washed out.

playbook.title: On snow, never brighten globally
playbook.how: Neutralize the blue cast and protect the brightest snow. Adding exposure after the fact wipes out the texture.
